item.title: Generation of large-amplitude squeezed cat states with near-unity efficiency
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Repeated QND-based measurement-induced cat amplification prepares large-amplitude cat states without post-selection on specific photon numbers; success probability reaches 80.64% after 6 rounds for GKP-breeding resources yielding at least 10 dB effective squeezing, scaling with target fidelity ℱ≈1−0.03/ntot for ntot≥3.

Grade 0.450 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Simon K. Yung, Matthew S. Winnel, Timothy C. Ralph, Jie Zhao

Figure

Schematic of the iterative cat amplification protocol and Wigner distributions across successive rounds, demonstrating increasing cat amplitude and breeding into approximate GKP states.

Asks

How can optical large-amplitude squeezed cat states suitable for Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill breeding protocols be generated with near-deterministic efficiency?

Before

Single-round 6 dB squeezer cat preparation achieves a success probability of 0.16% for ntot≥8.

But

Requires photon-number resolving detection and inline optical squeezing; susceptible to optical loss per squeezer and detector inefficiency.

Tools

quantum non-demolition (QND) interactions · photon-number resolving (PNR) detectors · inline optical squeezing · feedforward Gaussian displacement

Abstract

The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill encoding has emerged as a leading candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computation with continuous variables. For photonic architectures, the major challenge is preparing high-quality resource states, which can be deterministically synthesised from many large-amplitude cat states. Thus far, only modest-sized optical cat states have been prepared experimentally, and the implemented methods are highly probabilistic. We propose an all-optical scheme utilising quantum non-demolition interactions and photon-number measurements to prepare large-amplitude cat states with near-unity probability. Importantly, no particular photon-number outcome is postselected: all outcomes contribute to the accumulated photon number, with the protocol repeated until a required threshold is reached. We demonstrate that the scheme is robust to realistic levels of photon-loss, the dominant source of error in optical systems. Our results highlight the power of active Gaussian operations for state preparation and pave the way for efficient quantum error correction using bosonic codes.

item.title: Phase-sensitive avalanche quantum sensing of sub-shot-noise fields
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Trapped atomic cloud in cavity tuned to a parity-forbidden second-harmonic mode amplifies sub-shot-noise coherent displacement |αp|2=0.5 by over two orders of magnitude into macroscopic emission while preserving input optical phase.

Grade 0.448 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Nikolai D. Klimkin, Misha Ivanov

Figure

Normalized output field ⟨Fˆ⟩/⟨Fˆ2⟩vac versus time for input perturbation phases π/2, π, 3π/2, and 2π. Macroscopic emission rises well above shot noise while preserving the input π/2 phase increments.

Asks

Can avalanche amplification detect sub-shot-noise quantum light fluctuations without destroying phase information?

But

Numerical simulation of Ne=60 two-level atoms; classical driver flat-top envelope with peak Rabi frequency 0.1ω0 and CEP-averaged; ignores thermal bath and inter-atomic collisions.

Tools

Hierarchy of Pure States (HOPS) method · Tight-binding cavity waveguide model · Two-level atom ensemble model · Multimode Husimi function analysis

Abstract

Avalanche-based detection of small perturbations is commonplace in precision measurement devices from Geiger counters to single-photon avalanche detectors. Here, we expand this principle to sensing of light waves below the quantum shot noise limit, demonstrating numerically how atomic clouds trapped in photonic cavities can exhibit non-perturbative sensitivity to changes in the cavity field when the cavity mode is tuned to a parity-prohibited transition. We find that, when pumped by a continuous-wave laser, the atomic cloud creates emissions which amplify the initially sub-shot-noise fluctuation by two orders of magnitude. Crucially, this amplification is broadly tunable with respect to frequency and independent of atomic energy structure. Even more strikingly, our amplification mechanism preserves the phase imparted on the atoms by the original ultra-weak light wave, marking a qualitative improvement over conventional protocols. Our finding has implications for both quantum state characterization and detection of weak classical signals.

item.title: All-Microwave Multiqubit Gates
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Single-step (n+m) multiqubit gates implemented on transmon networks via cross-resonance drives without tunable couplers. Three-qubit gates reach simulated fidelities >99.9% in 60 ns.

Grade 0.433 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Guanqi Wang, Yao Song, Peng-Bo Li, Xiu-Hao Deng

Figure

Gate infidelity versus optimization iteration and target Pauli operation fidelity across three-qubit gates and larger multi-target configurations, showing convergence below 10−3.

Asks

How can single-step multiqubit gates with n control and m target transmons be implemented with all-microwave control without tunable couplers?

But

Numerical simulation only. Dispersive regime with shared or near-degenerate target frequencies and suppressed parasitic terms such as ZXX.

Tools

cross-resonance microwave drives · quad frame rotation · block diagonalization · gradient-based pulse optimization

Abstract

Implementing high-fidelity multiqubit gates is critical for reducing circuit depth in near-term quantum processors and fault-tolerant architectures. However, realizing multiqubit interactions and entanglement remains a critical challenge that limits the implementation of multiqubit gates. Here we propose an all-microwave scheme to realize single-step multiqubit gates incorporating n control and m target qubits, tailored for frequency-tunable superconducting transmon networks. By leveraging cross-resonance (CR) drives, this approach induces effective two-body ZX interactions that are significantly stronger than those achieved in conventional resonant regimes, circumventing the need for tunable couplers. The system's effective Hamiltonian is analytically derived using both quad frame rotation and rigorous block diagonalization. These combined theoretical methods facilitate the identification of optimal parameter regimes that simultaneously enhance desired target couplings and suppress parasitic higher-order terms, such as ZXX interactions. Through numerical simulations and gradient-based pulse-shape optimization, we demonstrate three-qubit gates achieving fidelities exceeding 99.9% within a 60 ns gate duration. Furthermore, we evaluate the fundamental scalability of this framework by extending the optimization to a five-qubit CXXXX architecture, confirming the physical viability of the multi-target driving scheme. Because these multiqubit operations naturally emulate stabilizer measurements, this architecture provides a hardware-efficient strategy for reducing the circuit depth of stabilizer-type operations by replacing sequential two-qubit gate decompositions with single-step multiqubit gates.

item.title: Parallel algebraic surgery for qLDPC codes with constant shuttling depth
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructs algebraic surgery directly over group algebras of cyclic lifted-product codes, yielding constant shuttling depth O(1) on 2D neutral-atom arrays. A syndrome cycle with 33 parallel logical measurements is roughly 2× faster than single-observable graph-based surgery schedules.

Grade 0.421 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits” · Tian-Gang Zhou, Boren Gu, Jens Eisert, Chen Zhao

Figure

Syndrome-extraction cycle times (broken into shuttling and gate times) and total qubit counts across lifted-product code instances (l=9,15,33), comparing memory, algebraic surgery, and graph-based surgery schedules.

Asks

Can the parallelism and reconfigurable connectivity of neutral-atom processors implement high-rate quantum LDPC logical operations without prohibitive shuttling overhead?

Before

Graph-based surgery auxiliary constructions require general ancilla matchings with O(log⁡w) shuttling depth on atom arrays and roughly double the memory cycle time.

But

Restricted to parallel measurements satisfying cyclic-symmetry or cyclically invariant subspace constraints; evaluated via numerical shuttling-time models and phenomenological/circuit noise simulations without experimental execution.

Tools

Lifted-product (LP) codes over F₂[x]/(x^l+1) · Acousto-optic deflector (AOD) shuttling · Stim circuit simulations · Relay-BP and BP-LSD decoders · QDistRnd distance estimator

Abstract

Reconfigurable atom arrays provide a promising platform for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes, but their computational advantage depends on whether logical operations can be implemented without incurring prohibitive shuttling and space overheads. We introduce algebraic surgery for lifted product codes, co-designing the logical measurements, auxiliary codes, and atom shuttling to enable hardware-efficient Pauli-product measurements. These protocols provide flexible logical addressability subject to the cyclic-symmetry constraint, enabling a broad class of parallel logical measurements, including canonical logical operators with heavily overlapping physical supports and joint measurements within or between code blocks even with different lift sizes, while achieving constant shuttling depth on neutral-atom processors under explicit layout assumptions. In a representative hardware-model benchmark, a cycle supporting 33 parallel canonical logical measurements is about 2× faster than the compared single-observable graph-based surgery schedules, with competitive qubit overhead. These shuttling and circuit-level simulations confirm that the algebraic structure of quantum low-density parity-check codes can be used not only to reduce space overhead, but also to simplify physical implementation and expand the set of efficiently accessible logical operations on neutral-atom processors.

item.title: CSS codes for Quantum Metrology with Discrete-time Error Correction
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Discrete-time CSS quantum error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling δω∝T−1 against perpendicular noise within an interrogation window scaling as tp∼1/τ, before crossing over to SQL-like scaling δω∝T−1/2. Single recovery applied solely at interrogation end yields zero metrological advantage.

Grade 0.409 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Ugnė Liaubaitė, Debora Ramacciotti, Robert Raußendorf

Figure

Frequency sensitivity versus total sensing time budget T for Steane and Shor codes across correction intervals τ. Sensitivity scales linearly (T−1) up to optimal interrogation time topt, then transitions to square-root scaling (T−1/2).

Asks

How does finite-frequency discrete error correction with Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes preserve parameter sensitivity and affect the Heisenberg-to-SQL crossover under perpendicular Markovian noise?

But

Instantaneous and ideal recovery operations; initial logical-plus state |+L⟩⊗k without noise optimization; local Z signal Hamiltonian and perpendicular Markovian X noise.

Tools

CSS stabilizer codes (Steane, Shor) · Adjoint Lindblad master equation · Discrete syndrome extraction and recovery map · Classical Fisher information of stabilizer projector

Abstract

The goal of quantum metrology is to estimate an unknown parameter with better-than-classical precision and, ideally, to attain Heisenberg scaling. In realistic settings, however, noise can substantially reduce this advantage and, in many cases, restore standard-quantum-limit-like performance. Preserving the quantum enhancement therefore requires noise-robust strategies, which can be implemented using quantum error correction. In this work, we develop and analyze a quantum-metrology protocol based on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. The main result is that, for noise perpendicular to the sensing Hamiltonian, discrete-time error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling over a finite interrogation-time window whose duration depends on the correction frequency. It is further shown that recovery applied only after the sensing evolution provides no metrological advantage over the corresponding uncorrected noisy protocol in the setup considered here. An analytical framework is developed for arbitrary CSS codes and applied to the Steane and Shor codes, for which the discrete-time corrected dynamics, the Heisenberg-like-to-SQL-like crossover, and the optimal interrogation time are determined and numerically analysed.

item.title: Proposal for matter-wave interferometry with a rare-earth-doped microparticle
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Proposed Mach-Zehnder matter-wave interferometer for a rare-earth-doped microparticle reaches up to 103 photons per beam splitter with millisecond coherence time. Mass-scaling keeps external decoherence rates constant or decreasing in the long-wavelength limit λ≫Δx.

Grade 0.408 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Chris Overstreet

Figure

Calculated background gas decoherence rate as a function of microparticle mass for 2ℏk and 1000ℏk momentum transfers at 10−6 Torr and 6 K.

Asks

How can matter-wave interference be observed for a microparticle without requiring ground-state cooling, orientational control, or ultrahigh vacuum?

Before

Gravitationally mediated entanglement requires mass ∼1012 amu, a factor of 107 higher than existing matter-wave interferometry.

But

Cryogenic environment (≈6 K) and moderate vacuum (10−6 Torr); microparticle material requires maximum phonon frequency ≲7 THz.

Tools

Mach-Zehnder geometry · two-photon Raman transitions · ⁶F_(1/2) state of Sm³⁺ in SrSe · Judd-Ofelt theory · buffer-gas cooling

Abstract

Matter-wave interferometers are sensitive probes of low energy physics and have been used for precise tests of gravity and quantum mechanics. These applications would benefit from interfering particles of higher mass, but observing the interference of a large particle is challenging due to the need to control its initial state and to avoid decoherence. Here we propose to demonstrate matter-wave interference of a microparticle with an embedded rare-earth ion. Optical transitions of the rare-earth ion will impart momentum to the microparticle's center of mass. The use of a time-symmetric interferometer geometry and a rare-earth ion state with angular momentum J = 1/2 will eliminate sensitivity to the initial conditions of the microparticle. We show that the rates of all relevant external decoherence mechanisms either decrease or remain constant as the microparticle mass is increased, allowing decoherence to be avoided by using sufficiently large particles. An apparatus at moderate vacuum levels will support microparticle interferometry with up to 10³ photons per beam splitter and millisecond coherence time. This demonstration will establish microparticle interferometry as a new platform for quantum sensing, improving searches for minimal modifications of quantum mechanics by up to four orders of magnitude in the near term and laying the foundation for future gravitational tests.

item.title: Quantum double lock-in detection via sequential orthogonal quantum mixing
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Single-interferometer quantum double lock-in detection extracts amplitude A, frequency ω, and initial phase β of an oscillating signal, achieving Heisenberg-limited precisions ΔA,Δω,Δβ∝1/N with an N-particle GHZ probe and interaction-based readout.

Grade 0.408 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Min Zhuang, Sijie Chen, Jiahao Huang, Chaohong Lee

Figure

Log-log scaling of measurement precisions ΔA, Δω, and Δβ versus particle number N, showing 1/N standard quantum limit for spin-coherent states and 1/N Heisenberg scaling for GHZ states.

Asks

Can quantum double lock-in detection extract full amplitude, frequency, and phase information from an unknown oscillating signal using a single quantum interferometry while achieving Heisenberg-limited precision?

Before

Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two separate quantum interferometers, each requiring state preparation and readout (was ∝1/N scaling without entanglement).

But

Theoretical derivation assuming instantaneous π pulses and noiseless state initialization. Gaussian detection noise σ=0.5N degrades scaling to between SQL and Heisenberg limit.

Tools

Periodic dynamical decoupling (PDD) sequences · Carr-Purcell (CP) sequences · Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states · Fast Fourier transform (FFT) / Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) analysis

Abstract

High-precision measurement of oscillating signal is a ubiquitous issue in fundamental science and a critical task in practical technologies. In quantum metrology, quantum lock-in detection provide an efficient method for measuring such signal. In general, when the initial phase of the oscillating signal is unknown,quantum double lock-in detection can effectively extract complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two individual quantum interferometry, each of which must undergo state preparation and readout. However, the time for state preparation and readout need not be negligible in practical experiments. In particular, the time for state preparation is longer than the time for sensing. To save experimental resources, it is challenging to achieve quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry while still extracting complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Here, we present a general protocol for achieving a quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry under a sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences. In particular, if the input state is a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and two interaction-based operations are applied during interferometry, the measurement precisions for frequency, amplitude, and initial phase can both approach the Heisenberg limit. Our study paves a new way for measuring oscillating signals with a single quantum interferometry, and provides a feasible method for achieving Heisenberg-limited detection of alternating signals.

item.title: Entangling Atomic Quantum Memories Using High-Order Modulated Coherent States
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Square-root-measurement-inspired 16-QAM receiver achieves 1.75 ebits per mode at 0.5 dB end-to-end loss, 3.8 dB below the two-way assisted single-half-link PLOB capacity. Variational 32-outcome POVM increases 4-QAM rate by 4.0% over the square-root measurement to 1.1289 ebits per mode.

Grade 0.404 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Chaohan Cui, Prajit Dhara, Saikat Guha

Figure

Entanglement distribution rate per mode versus end-to-end channel loss Lch (dB) for various M-QAM orders compared to single-photon baselines and the PLOB capacity limit.

Asks

Can high-order coherent-state modulation distribute multiple ebits per optical mode between stationary atomic memories through a collective midpoint measurement?

Before

was at most 0.46 ebits per mode at 0.5 dB end-to-end loss for single-photon baseline links

But

Pure-loss channels; advantage over single-photon protocols requires per-interface loss ≲0.2 dB and systematic phase error |δϕ|≲0.2π; physical linear-optical implementation of the collective midpoint POVM remains open.

Tools

square-root measurement (SRM) POVM · reflective cavity qubit-photon interfaces · M-QAM coherent-state modulation · two-way coherent information (hashing bound) · variational POVM optimization

Abstract

High-order coherent-state modulation with reflective cavity-coupled atomic memories can distribute multiple heralded ebits per transmitted optical mode, but requires a collective midpoint POVM optimized for maximum distillable entanglement rather than minimum-error state discrimination. An SRM-inspired 16-QAM receiver reaches 1.75 ebits per mode at 0.5~dB end-to-end loss, 3.8~dB below the half-link capacity benchmark. For 4-QAM, a variational POVM with more outcomes than constellation points improves the SRM rate by 4.0% yet remains below capacity, revealing measurement-design headroom. The advantage over single-qubit-per-mode midpoint protocols persists for per-interface loss <0.2~dB and calibrated phase error <0.2π.
